title: Mandela and the Miracle of 1994

cards.h: A prisoner who became a president
cards.b:
Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison for opposing apartheid. He walked out in 1990 and became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994. His story is one of the most famous of the modern world.

Mandela's life also shows the hard choices of a freedom struggle: violence, negotiation, forgiveness and power. The lessons are still debated.

Mandela was born in 1918 in the Eastern Cape. He studied law and, in the 1940s, joined the African National Congress. In 1952 he helped lead the Defiance Campaign, in which volunteers broke apartheid laws in peaceful protest.

Mandela was sometimes called the "Black Pimpernel" in the 1960s, for he moved in secret from place to place before his arrest. His early years show a man who first believed in disciplined, peaceful protest.

After Sharpeville in 1960, the ANC decided that peaceful protest alone would not work. In 1961 Mandela helped found Umkhonto we Sizwe, the armed wing of the movement. Its early campaign used sabotage against state targets, while avoiding deliberate killing of civilians.

The decision was controversial, and historians still debate it. It shows how a movement can change its methods when peaceful protest is answered with force.

Nelson Mandela at the Rivonia trial (1964)

At the trial Mandela spoke for hours about the aims of the ANC and the reasons for its armed struggle. He ended with a famous line that he was prepared to die for the ideal of a free and democratic society.

The speech is one of the most important political statements of the 20th century.
Mandela spent most of his adult life in prison or underground. His release came after years of pressure, and his election came after tough negotiations.

Mandela spent most of his imprisonment on Robben Island, off Cape Town. He worked in a lime quarry, where the glare damaged his eyesight. He studied, wrote letters and built a discipline among prisoners that became legendary.

Prison changed him. He gained patience, and he learned to read his jailers. He also became a symbol for millions who had never met him.

Mandela is often shown as a saint who forgave everything and never made mistakes. Monuments and speeches make him a figure of moral perfection.

Historians argue that his life was more complicated. He led an armed movement, and his later government faced criticism for its economic policy and for the slow pace of land reform. Seeing him as a human leader gives a fuller picture than the saint image.

Negotiations between the ANC and the National Party, led by F. W. de Klerk, lasted several years. Both men shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. The first democratic elections, in April 1994, gave the ANC about 62 per cent of the vote, and Mandela took office in May.

The new constitution included a bill of rights. The country faced huge problems of poverty, housing and inequality, but the peaceful transfer of power was a historic achievement.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, heard testimony from victims and perpetrators between 1996 and 1998. It offered amnesty to those who told the full truth about political crimes.

The commission is praised by some and criticised by others. Victims' families often felt justice was incomplete. Historians argue about its real effects, but its work remains a model studied around the world.

Mandela served one term as president and then stepped down in 1999. He was one of the few African leaders of his era to leave office by choice, and he became an elder statesman who spoke on AIDS, poverty and peace.

His restraint helped the new democracy take root. Historians argue about how much of that was personal and how much was built into the new system.

In 1991 India faced a serious balance-of-payments crisis. It borrowed from the IMF, and the government of P. V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as finance minister, began a programme of economic liberalisation.

The two countries were both changing in the early 1990s. South Africa was moving from apartheid to democracy, and India was opening its economy to the world. Both made deep changes in the same years.

Five things to remember
  1. Mandela was sentenced to life in 1964 at the Rivonia trial.
  2. He was released in February 1990.
  3. The first democratic elections were held in April 1994.
  4. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission ran from 1996 to 1998.
  5. He stepped down after one term in 1999.
Think about it
  • Can a leader who once used violence become a symbol of peace?
  • What does forgiveness owe to justice?
